  • A read decompresses. values(), value_map(), element_map(), project().by(), order().by(), a jpath read, a result: each decompresses the value it reads (about 1.5 to 3 GB/s, below). A read that never touches the field costs nothing.
  • A filter on such a field decompresses every candidate. has("bio", TextP.containing("Rust")) reads the text of every vertex it tests. Filter on other properties first. A property index on the field serves equality and ranges without reading the candidates, but it holds the plain text (the memory compression saved).
  • A write compresses a string at a rule path (with the rule's dictionary). Only the touched top-level property is looked at; with no rule for the element's labels a write costs one lookup.
  • The disk stays plain. Snapshots, the write-ahead log, GraphSON and GraphML hold the plain text: the persistence layer compresses whole chunks and large WAL records already, compressing single values twice would only cost CPU. A load compresses the rule paths again in one pass.

Rules

A rule is a definition of kind compression in the graph's catalog, next to the saved queries. It has:

FieldMeaningDefault
namean identifier, unique among the rulesrequired
element"vertex" or "edge""vertex"
labelthe label the rule applies to (it need not exist yet)required
patha property name or a jpath of names: "cv", "details.career.cv", jpath("$['a b'].c"); no index ([0], [-1]): arrays are not compressed in this versionrequired
codec"lz4" (the only codec of this version)"lz4"
min_bytesstrings shorter than this (UTF-8 bytes) stay plain; 1 to 16 MiB256
dictionarybuild a dictionary from the rule's valuestrue
  • Any number of rules: several paths on one label, the same path on different labels, vertex and edge labels. One rule per element kind, label and path: a second one is refused (DefinitionError::Conflict, its help names drop_compression).
  • Several labels of one vertex: every label's rules apply; when two labels have a rule for the same path, the first label in label order wins (the same rule as schema coercion).
  • A label change (add_vertex_label/remove_vertex_label, set_edge_label) compresses what a new label's rules cover and decompresses what no rule covers any more.
  • Only strings are compressed. A number, an object or an array at a rule path stays as it is.

The explicit pass

Defining a rule, redefining it with other parameters, dropping it and loading the catalog run the pass over the rule's label in the same commit: every value at the old and the new path is re-encoded (compressed when it qualifies, decompressed when it no longer does). g.recompress(name) runs it again on demand and rebuilds the dictionary, for example after much data was added to a rule that was defined on an empty label. The pass changes no data: a commit hook sees only the SetDefinition of the rule, and a recompress alone commits nothing.

Dictionaries

With dictionary: true the pass builds a dictionary from a sample of the rule's current values (in id order, up to 1 KiB of each value, up to 64 KiB, the LZ4 window) and compresses with it, which helps short and similar texts most. A dictionary is in memory only: a load builds it again. A value written before a dictionary exists (a rule on an empty label) is compressed without one until the next recompress or load. Every compressed value carries its dictionary, so it stays readable when the rule changes.

g.compressions() lists each rule with compressed_values, plain_bytes, stored_bytes and dictionary_bytes. g.memory_usage() (and MemoryStats) adds compressed_values, compressed_plain_bytes, compressed_stored_bytes and compression_dictionary_bytes; property_bytes counts the compressed (stored) size.

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
use graphersal::prelude::*;
use graphersal::{catalog::CompressionDefinition, storage::ElementKind};

let mut graph = TraversalGraph::new();
let rule = CompressionDefinition::new(ElementKind::Vertex, "customer", "details.career.cv")
    .unwrap()
    .with_min_bytes(512)
    .with_dictionary(false);
graph.traversal_mut().define_compression("customer_cv", rule).unwrap();
}

Authorization: a rule is the resource Definition { kind: compression, name }: define asks Create (Update when it replaces one), drop Delete, recompress Update, listing Read. No data request is made (the logical data does not change). AccessPolicy::read_only(), the MCP read-only mode and a saved query (which always runs read-only) cannot change rules.

The catalog file: rules travel with the saved queries in one catalog file ({"definitions": [..]}, the playground's Catalog ▾ ▸ Save catalog, the dev server's GET /api/catalog/export); loading it stores the rules and compresses their values at once. A snapshot and a Store carry the catalog, so a rule survives every store operation (WAL replay, checkpoint, fork, backup, restore, repair, rollback); the files hold plain values, and the load compresses again. A version that does not know the kind keeps the rule unchanged and only loses the compression (the definition is not critical).

In the playground, Catalog ▾ ▸ Compression lists the rules with their statistics (here 400 customer biographies, about 1 KiB each) and defines, edits, recompresses and drops them:

Measured

On a generated CV-like corpus of 5,000 texts of 2 to 20 KB (55 MB: section headers, sentences from a 200-word vocabulary, company names, years and numbers), Apple M-series, --release (compressed_property_tests::measure_ratio_and_throughput, an #[ignore]d test):

Stored / plainDictionaryDefine pass (compress)Read (decompress + materialize)
LZ40.52none451 MB/s2,741 MB/s
LZ4 with dictionary0.4264 KiB328 MB/s1,626 MB/s

The compression figures include a round-trip check of every value (a compressed value is verified once when it is made, so reading it back cannot fail). A highly repetitive corpus (a dozen phrases recombined) compresses to 0.07 (0.05 with a dictionary).

Vectors

New to embeddings? Embeddings and Vector Search is the task-oriented tour: semantic search, filtered search, GraphRAG and recommendations, in the playground with toy vectors and in Python with a real model. This page is the reference.

A vector is a fixed-length list of numbers stored as one value: an embedding of a text, an image or a node, as a language or vision model computes it. A property holds a vector, not a list that happens to contain numbers, and the engine stores it compactly, converts it between element kinds and compares it as one value. Vectors are a Graphersal extension: TinkerPop has no vector type.

Embeddings are computed outside the engine. A step that called an embedding model would make a query depend on a network service, could not be rolled back (a paid call stays paid) and would not run in the browser playground. The host computes them, in Python, in an MCP tool or in a server, and writes them as ordinary property values.

type_of(vector([0.12, -0.5, 0.33]))   // "Vector"
vector([0.12, -0.5, 0.33]).dimension   // 3
vector([0.12, -0.5, 0.33], "i8").element   // "i8"
g.inject(vector([0.5, 1.0])).is(P.typeOf(GType.VECTOR)).count().next()   // 1

Element kinds and quantization

A vector has 1 to 65 536 components, all of one element kind:

ElementA componentBytes per component768 components
f32 (default)an IEEE single-precision float43 KiB
f16an IEEE half-precision float21.5 KiB
i8an 8-bit code times one f32 scale per vector (value = code * scale)1768 B
bitone sign bit: 1.0 for a set bit, -1.0 otherwise1/896 B

A list of 768 numbers as a plain array takes about 24 KiB; the same vector as f32 3 KiB.

Quantization converts a vector to another element kind, to save memory at a small cost in precision:

  • f32 to f16 rounds every component to the nearest half value (ties to even). A component beyond the half range (65 504) is an error, never an infinity.
  • f32 to i8 is symmetric scalar quantization: scale = max |x| / 127, code = round(x / scale) in -127..=127. A zero vector has scale 0.
  • f32 to bit keeps the sign: a component > 0 sets its bit (binary quantization).
  • Every other conversion goes through the f32 values, so quantize("f32") dequantizes.
vector([0.5, -1.0, 0.25]).quantize("bit").to_list()   // [1.0, -1.0, 1.0]
vector([0.5, -1.0, 0.25]).quantize("f16").to_list()   // [0.5, -1.0, 0.25]
g.inject(vector([0.5, -1.0, 0.25])).quantize("i8").next().element   // "i8"
vector([1e10], "f16")   // fails: the component is beyond the range of an f16 vector

All four kinds are part of the value type and of every file format from the start, so storing a property quantized is a choice of the data, never a format change.

Building vectors

  • vector(list) builds an f32 vector of a list of numbers; vector(list, kind) quantizes it to "f16", "i8" or "bit".
  • The as_vector() step converts a list of numbers in a traversal (a stored list, a fold()); a vector passes, null stays null.
  • A schema that declares the property as a vector converts a written list on write (below).

A vector never holds NaN or an infinity (it would break ordering and comparison); -0.0 is kept and equals 0.0. An empty list, a component that is not a number and more than 65 536 components are errors:

g.inject([0.5, 1]).as_vector().next()   // vector([0.5, 1.0])
g.inject(1, 2, 3).fold().as_vector().next().dimension   // 3
vector([])   // fails: a vector has 1 to 65536 components
vector([1, "x"])   // fails: component 1 is not a number

A vector prints as its DSL literal, which evaluates back to the same vector (an i8 or bit vector shows its dequantized values and its kind): vector([0.5, 1.0]), vector([0.503937, -1.0], "i8"). to_string() and the step names in .profile() cut it after 16 components, like a list. In a script a vector has the getters element and dimension and the methods quantize(kind) and to_list() (the values as floats).

Writing, filtering and ordering

A vector is written like any other value, and has() compares it by value: the same element kind, the same dimension and equal components. A list is never equal to a vector, and an f16 vector never equals an f32 one, even with the same values:

g.add_v("doc").property("title", "Graphs").property("emb", vector([0.1, 0.9])).iterate();
g.add_v("doc").property("title", "Vectors").property("emb", vector([0.8, 0.2])).iterate();
g.v().has("emb", vector([0.1, 0.9])).values("title").next();   // "Graphs"
g.v().has("emb", [0.1, 0.9]).count().next();   // 0
g.v().has_label("doc").order().by("emb").values("title").to_list()   // ["Graphs", "Vectors"]

Vectors order (a Graphersal extension) after the dates and before strings; among themselves by element kind (f32, f16, i8, bit), then by dimension, then component by component. A vector is one value in the local steps (count(Scope.local) is 1, unfold() passes it), and min()/max() refuse it.

A property index never holds vectors: has(key, vector) on an indexed key reads the elements by a scan, with the same result.

Quantize an existing property with one write per element, then declare the new element in the schema (g.patch_schema(..), below). This works as shown while no schema declares the property; when the schema already declares it as f32 (mode open or closed), a write is converted back to f32 and the new element is refused while f32 data remains: the migration recipe for that case (mode none for the rewrite, one unit) is in Embeddings and Vector Search.

g.add_v("doc").property("emb", vector([0.5, -1.0, 0.25])).iterate();
g.v().has_label("doc").has("emb").property("emb", __.values("emb").quantize("i8")).iterate();
g.v().values("emb").next().element   // "i8"

Vectors in a schema

A schema declares a vector property as an array with the custom format vector:

{"type": "array", "format": "vector", "element": "i8", "dimension": 768, "metric": "cosine"}
  • element (default f32) and dimension (optional: any dimension) are checked exactly: a stored vector of another kind or length does not conform. metric (cosine, dot, l2, hamming) is an annotation: the metric the vectors are meant to be compared with, which similarity() and nearest() use when the query names none (Metrics). It never changes or checks any data.
  • items is not allowed next to the format (the components are numbers of the element kind).
  • Another JSON Schema validator ignores the unknown format and keywords and sees an array of numbers, which is what a vector exports as. The schema visualizer's per-label JSON Schema (visualize("jsonschema")) spells out items and minItems/maxItems for it.

In mode open or closed, a list of numbers written to the property becomes a vector of the declared element, and a vector of another element is quantized to it: a property is stored quantized from the start, whatever the host sends. The dimension is never changed:

g.set_schema(#{mode: "open", vertices: #{doc: #{schema: #{type: "object", properties: #{
  emb: #{type: "array", format: "vector", element: "i8", dimension: 3}}}}}});
g.add_v("doc").property("emb", [0.5, -1.0, 0.25]).iterate();
g.add_v("doc").property("emb", vector([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])).iterate();
g.v().values("emb").to_list().map(|v| v.element)   // ["i8", "i8"]

On that graph, g.add_v("doc").property("emb", [1.0, 2.0]) fails with "Type mismatch on vertex 'doc.emb': expected vector<i8, 3>, got vector<i8, 2>", and its help names the conversion (values("emb").as_vector().quantize("i8")).

infer_schema() reports a vector as such, with its dimension when every vector of that element at the position has the same one. diff_schema() counts a change of element or dimension (and a list turned into a vector, or back) as incompatible, since the stored data no longer conforms; dropping dimension (any dimension) is compatible. A saved query takes a vector parameter the same way: params: #{q: #{schema: #{type: "array", format: "vector", element: "f32", dimension: 768}}}; a list argument is converted to the declared vector.

Similarity

similarity() scores a vector against a query vector q and yields a float64. It is a map step in two forms:

FormScores
similarity(key, q[, metric])the vector property key (a name or a jpath(..)) of the incoming element (or map)
similarity(q[, metric])the incoming value itself, a vector (values("emb").similarity(q), a computed vector)

q is a vector, a list of numbers (made an f32 vector when the step is built), or an anonymous traversal run on each incoming traverser whose first result is the query (__.select("q")). The key form drops an element without the property or whose value is not a vector; the value form drops null and fails on any other value that is not a vector.

g.add_v("doc").property("title", "Graphs").property("emb", vector([0.6, 0.8])).iterate();
g.add_v("doc").property("title", "Vectors").property("emb", vector([1.0, 0.0])).iterate();
g.v().has_label("doc").similarity("emb", vector([1.0, 0.0])).to_list();   // [0.6000000095367428, 1.0]
g.v().has_label("doc").values("emb").similarity([0.0, 0.0], "l2").to_list();   // [1.000000023841858, 1.0]
g.v().has_label("doc")
 .project("title", "score").by("title").by(__.similarity("emb", vector([1.0, 0.0])))
 .to_list()

Metrics

MetricScoreCloser isVectors
cosine (default)the dot product over the product of the norms, -1 to 1; 0.0 when either vector is zero (never NaN)higherany kind except bit against non-bit
dotthe dot producthigheras cosine
l2the Euclidean distancesmalleras cosine
hammingthe number of differing bitssmallerbit vectors only

The metric is the step's argument if it names one; otherwise the metric annotation the stored schema declares for the property (a top-level name on a vertex or edge, by the element's labels like a write; for the value form, the property a values("emb") reference points to), and cosine without one. A computed vector, a jpath key and a map have no declaration: cosine.

Scores are exact: every component is read from the stored kind (an f16 or i8 vector dequantized, bits counted) and summed in f64, in a fixed order, so the same vectors always give the same score. Vectors of different element kinds compare through their values: an i8 property can be searched with an f32 query. A bit vector compares only with another bit vector (for which the dot product, cosine and distance follow exactly from the Hamming distance, the components being ±1). Two vectors of different dimensions are an error, never truncated:

g.inject(vector([1.0, 0.0])).similarity(vector([1.0, 0.0, 0.0])).next()   // fails: vectors of dimensions 2 and 3 cannot be compared
g.inject(vector([1.0, -1.0], "bit")).similarity(vector([1.0, -1.0])).next()   // fails: a bit vector compares only with another bit vector
g.inject(vector([1.0, -1.0], "bit")).similarity(vector([1.0, 1.0], "bit"), "hamming").next()   // 1.0

Exact search: nearest()

nearest(key, q, k[, #{metric: ".."}]) keeps the k incoming elements whose vector property key is closest to q, best first (the highest cosine or dot, the smallest l2 or hamming). It is an exact search: every incoming element is scored, with a bounded heap of k (O(n log k), never a full sort).

  • Elements without the property, or whose value is not a vector, are skipped.
  • Equal scores keep the input order, the earlier element first: the answer is deterministic, the same in a live graph, a view at a commit and a fork.
  • q is a vector, a list of numbers or a traversal. A traversal runs for every scored element and must give the same vector each time (one query per search, "more like this" below); a query that depends on the element fails and names similarity(), which scores each element against its own vector.
  • The metric follows the same rule as for similarity(). Without a metric argument, elements whose labels declare different metrics fail: one search ranks with one metric.
  • Bulk counts as in limit(): a traverser that stands for n equal ones is n results, cut at k.
  • .profile() shows the step as written, nearest("emb", vector([..]), 10, #{metric: "l2"}); the deadline (evaluationTimeout) and a cancel stop it while it scores.
g.add_v("doc").property("title", "Graph databases 101").property("emb", vector([0.9, 0.1, 0.0])).iterate();
g.add_v("doc").property("title", "Vector search").property("emb", vector([0.1, 0.9, 0.1])).iterate();
g.add_v("doc").property("title", "Indexes").property("emb", vector([0.6, 0.6, 0.2], "i8")).iterate();
g.add_v("doc").property("title", "Draft").iterate();
g.v().has_label("doc").nearest("emb", vector([1.0, 0.2, 0.0]), 2).values("title").to_list();   // ["Graph databases 101", "Indexes"]
g.v().has_label("doc").nearest("emb", [0.0, 1.0, 0.0], 1, #{metric: "l2"}).values("title").next()   // "Vector search"

nearest() is the same as ordering by the score and keeping k, which is how to get the scores along with the elements:

g.add_v("doc").property("title", "a").property("emb", vector([1.0, 0.0])).iterate();
g.add_v("doc").property("title", "b").property("emb", vector([0.6, 0.8])).iterate();
let q = vector([1.0, 0.1]);
g.v().has_label("doc").nearest("emb", q, 2)
 .project("title", "score").by("title").by(__.similarity("emb", q))
 .to_list()

Filtered search

Filter first, then search: has_label() and has() before nearest() reduce what it scores (a has_label() folds into v() as usual, a property index serves a has()), and a where() can filter by the graph around each element:

g.add_v("team").property("name", "engineering").as("eng")
 .add_v("doc").property("title", "Design").property("lang", "en").property("year", 2026)
   .property("emb", vector([0.9, 0.1])).add_e("owned_by").to("eng")
 .add_v("doc").property("title", "Entwurf").property("lang", "de").property("year", 2026)
   .property("emb", vector([0.9, 0.1])).add_e("owned_by").to("eng")
 .iterate();
g.v().has_label("doc")
 .has("lang", "en").has("year", P.gte(2026))
 .where(__.out("owned_by").has("name", "engineering"))
 .nearest("emb", vector([1.0, 0.0]), 5)
 .values("title").to_list()   // ["Design"]

GraphRAG: a vector hit, then the graph

Retrieval-augmented generation over a graph finds the chunks nearest to the question's embedding and expands along the edges to build the context:

g.add_v("doc").property("title", "Graphersal").as("d")
 .add_v("entity").property("name", "Rhai").as("e")
 .add_v("chunk").property("text", "Graphersal runs Gremlin in Rhai.").property("emb", vector([0.9, 0.2]))
   .add_e("part_of").to("d")
 .add_e("mentions").from("d").to("e")
 .iterate();
g.v().has_label("chunk").nearest("emb", vector([1.0, 0.1]), 5).as("hit")
 .out("part_of").as("doc")
 .out("mentions").has_label("entity").as("ent")
 .select("hit", "doc", "ent").by("text").by("title").by("name")
 .to_list()

The embedding of the question comes from the host (the model is never called by the engine), as a query parameter or the argument of a saved query: params: #{q: #{schema: #{type: "array", format: "vector", dimension: 384}}} with the body g.v().has_label("chunk").nearest("emb", q, k). MCP clients and the AI Chat call such a query with run_saved_query.

More like this

The query vector can come from the graph itself: label it, then search with __.select(..):

g.add_v("doc").property("id", "d42").property("emb", vector([1.0, 0.0])).iterate();
g.add_v("doc").property("id", "d7").property("emb", vector([0.9, 0.1])).iterate();
g.add_v("doc").property("id", "d9").property("emb", vector([0.0, 1.0])).iterate();
g.v().has("id", "d42").as("me").values("emb").as("q")
 .v().has_label("doc").where(P.neq("me"))
 .nearest("emb", __.select("q"), 2)
 .values("id").to_list()   // ["d7", "d9"]

Recommendations with vector_mean()

vector_mean() is a reducing barrier (like mean()): the component-wise mean of the incoming vectors, as an f32 vector. An incoming list of vectors (fold()) counts each of its vectors, null is skipped, quantized vectors count with their values, an empty stream gives no result, and vectors of different dimensions fail. local(__.unfold().vector_mean()) averages each list on its own. The mean of what a user liked is a taste vector to search with:

g.add_v("user").property("name", "u7").as("u")
 .add_v("article").property("title", "Graphs").property("emb", vector([1.0, 0.0])).as("a")
 .add_v("article").property("title", "Trees").property("emb", vector([0.8, 0.4])).as("b")
 .add_v("article").property("title", "Cooking").property("emb", vector([0.0, 1.0]))
 .add_v("article").property("title", "Forests").property("emb", vector([0.9, 0.3]))
 .add_e("liked").from("u").to("a").add_e("liked").from("u").to("b").add_e("read").from("u").to("a")
 .add_e("read").from("u").to("b")
 .iterate();
g.v().has("name", "u7").out("liked").values("emb").fold().vector_mean().as("taste")
 .v().has_label("article")
 .where(__.in("read").has("name", "u7").count().is(0))
 .nearest("emb", __.select("taste"), 1)
 .values("title").next()   // "Forests"

Performance

The search is an exact scan: its time grows with the number of scored elements times the dimension, and it needs no index, so it costs nothing to keep up to date and answers the same at every commit, mark and snapshot. Measured with the bench nearest_10k_x_384 (cargo bench -p graphersal --bench graph --features io,script,display,serde -- nearest_10k_x_384): 10 000 vertices with a random 384-dimensional embedding, v().has_label("doc").nearest("emb", q, 10), on an Apple M3:

Stored elementMetricMedianPer vector
f32cosine1.3 ms130 ns
f16cosine2.3 ms230 ns
i8cosine1.8 ms180 ns
bithamming0.21 ms21 ns

So about 13 ms per 100 000 f32 vectors of 384 components: enough for most in-memory graphs, and a filter before the search (above) scores fewer. There is no approximate (ANN) index yet (see Current Limitations).

Quantization: memory against accuracy

A quantized property takes less memory and gives approximately the same answers. Measured by the test quantized_search_recall_against_f32 on 2 000 random 128-dimensional vectors (20 queries, recall@10 against the f32 search with cosine); random vectors are the hardest case, real embeddings usually keep more:

Stored asBytes per 384 componentsrecall@10
f321 5361.00 (exact)
f167681.00
i8384 (+ 4 for the scale)0.99
bit (hamming)480.30
bit top 100, re-ranked by f3248 + 1 5360.74

Bit vectors are a coarse, very fast prefilter: keep both properties and re-rank the prefilter's hits exactly, nearest("emb_bit", q.quantize("bit"), 100, #{metric: "hamming"}) followed by nearest("emb", q, 10).

Storage and exchange

FormatA vector
Graphersal's binary format (snapshots, the Store, the journal)its own value tag: the element kind, the dimension, for i8 the scale, then the packed components (format spec 3)
Serialized ChangeSetexact, tagged: {"@type": "graphersal:Vector", "@value": {"element": "f32", "data": [..]}} (Transactions)
JSON results, to_json()the list of its values (an i8 or bit vector dequantized)
GraphSON exporta g:List of g:Float, which TinkerGraph loads
GraphSON importa list stays a list; it becomes a vector where the target schema declares one (mode open/closed); the exact graphersal:Vector tag is read too (GraphSON)
GraphMLthe JSON text of the list; a vector again where the target graph's schema declares one (any mode)

Exporting an i8 or bit vector as its values loses nothing that matters: a declared i8 property quantizes them back to the same codes. memory_usage() counts a vector's components exactly (plus a small header), and the memory budget of a query estimates them the same way.

From Python

A vector property is a graphersal.Vector in Python, built from a list of numbers or from any one-dimensional float32/float64 buffer such as a numpy array (the extension does not depend on numpy):

import numpy as np
from graphersal import Graph, Vector

g = Graph()
emb = np.array([0.12, -0.5, 0.33], dtype=np.float32)      # model.encode(text) in practice
g.execute('g.add_v("doc").property("emb", e).iterate()', params={"e": Vector(emb)})
v = g.query('g.v().values("emb").next()')                # graphersal.Vector
v.element, v.dimension, v.tolist()                       # ('f32', 3, [0.12, -0.5, 0.33])
Vector(emb, element="i8")                                # quantized, 1 byte per component

q = np.array([0.1, -0.4, 0.3], dtype=np.float32)          # the question's embedding
g.query('g.v().nearest("emb", q, 10).to_list()', params={"q": q})

A one-dimensional float32/float64 numpy array passed as a parameter arrives as an f32 vector, like Vector(array). See the Python binding's README for the details.

In the playground and the CLI

The result table shows a vector as vector[768 f32] with an expandable preview of its first values; the JSON view holds all of them. The property editor edits a vector as a JSON list of numbers (a declared vector property offers the type vector). The CLI's tables show the kind and the first values (vector[768 f32] [0.012, -0.5, 0.33, 0.1, …]), and a final vector prints as its literal.

Dates and Times

Graphersal has five date and time types. They are values of their own, like numbers and UUIDs: a property holds a date, not a string that looks like one, and a query compares, sorts and computes with it. The model follows PostgreSQL and the SQL standard; the part TinkerPop defines (datetime(), asDate(), dateAdd(), dateDiff(), DT.second to DT.day) behaves exactly as TinkerPop 3.8 specifies it (TinkerPop compatibility).

The five types

Graphersal (type_of, GType)What it isLiteralPostgreSQLSQL standardPythonTinkerPop / java.time
datetime (GType.DATETIME)an instant with the UTC offset it was written withdatetime("2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00")timestamptz (keeps no offset)TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONEaware datetime.datetimedatetime, OffsetDateTime
localdatetime (GType.LOCALDATETIME)a wall-clock date and time, no zonelocaldatetime("2023-08-02T09:30")timestampTIMESTAMPnaive datetime.datetimeLocalDateTime
date (GType.DATE)a calendar daydate("2023-08-02")dateDATEdatetime.dateLocalDate
time (GType.TIME)a time of day, no zonetime("09:30:15.5")timeTIMEnaive datetime.timeLocalTime
duration (GType.DURATION)months, days and microseconds, each with its own signduration("P1Y2M3DT4H")intervalINTERVALdatetime.timedelta, or graphersal.Interval with monthsDuration, Period
type_of(datetime("2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00"))   // "datetime"
date("2024-02-29").day   // 29
duration("P1Y2M3DT4H").months   // 14
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T09:30Z")).is(P.typeOf(GType.DATETIME)).count().next()   // 1
  • Resolution: one microsecond for every type, as in PostgreSQL and Python. TinkerPop's millisecond views (as_number() of a datetime, date_diff()) round down to milliseconds.
  • Range: the years -9999 to 9999 in the proleptic Gregorian calendar (date("-0044-03-15") is year 44 BC counted astronomically, year 0 = 1 BC). A value outside the range, or a result that would leave it, is an error, never a wrapped value.
  • Offsets: a datetime keeps its offset (±18:00, whole seconds) and shows it, unlike PostgreSQL's timestamptz, which keeps only the instant. A time zone is never stored in a value: operations take one (Time Zones).
  • A duration is not normalized: P1M, P30D and PT720H are three different values. A month has no fixed length and a day is not always 24 hours in a time zone, so the three fields stay apart, as in PostgreSQL's interval.
  • No guessing: a string stays a string whatever it looks like. A date comes from a constructor, a conversion step (Conversions), a schema that declares the property (Schema), a typed value in a file (Storage and Exchange) or a Python datetime (From Python).

Script values

In a script each type is a value of its own Rhai type with getters and operators:

TypeGetters
datetimeyear, month, day, hour, minute, second, microsecond (on its own wall clock), offset (seconds), epoch_millis
localdatetimeyear, month, day, hour, minute, second, microsecond
dateyear, month, day
timehour, minute, second, microsecond
durationmonths, days, micros
let d = datetime("2023-08-02T09:30:15.25+02:00"); [d.hour, d.offset, d.microsecond]   // [9, 7200, 250000]
datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z") + duration("P1M")   // datetime("2023-09-02T12:00:00Z")
date("2023-08-02") - date("2023-01-01")   // duration("P213D")
time("10:00") - time("09:30")   // duration("PT30M")
datetime("2023-08-02T09:30+02:00").as_string()   // "2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00"

+ and - with a duration work as date_add() does; the difference of two values of one type is a duration (two datetimes or localdatetimes give days of 24 hours and a time part, two dates days, two times the elapsed time). as_string() is the canonical text, to_string() the DSL literal. A value printed or shown as a script value is its literal (date("2023-08-02")); tables, JSON and the playground show the canonical text.

The pages of this part

  • Comparing and Sorting: equality by instant, field-wise durations, the order of types.
  • Text Formats: the canonical output, what is read, strict and lenient input.
  • Time Zones: the bundled IANA database, offsets, daylight saving.
  • Arithmetic: date_add(), date_diff(), age().
  • Truncation and Parts: date_trunc(), date_part().
  • Conversions: as_date(), as_duration(), as_number(), as_string().
  • now() and today(): the evaluation's start time and how a host pins it.
  • Dates in a Schema: the date formats, bounds and coercion.
  • Storage and Exchange: the binary format, GraphSON, GraphML, change sets.
  • From Python: the datetime mapping.
  • TinkerPop Compatibility: what is TinkerPop and what is an extension.

The steps have generated reference pages: as_date, as_duration, date_add, date_diff, age, date_trunc, date_part, at_zone and as_local; the constructors, now(), today() and DT are on Functions, Tokens and Values.

Comparing and Sorting

Every comparison of dates goes through one set of rules: == in a script, the predicates (P.eq, P.gt, P.between, P.within, ...), dedup(), group() and group_count() keys, order(), min()/max() and the schema bounds.

datetime: by its instant

Two datetimes are equal when they are the same instant, whatever their offsets (12:00Z equals 14:00+02:00). This is PostgreSQL's equality and TinkerPop's ("dates are evaluated based on the numerical comparison of Unix Epoch time"). The offset is kept and shown, but never compared:

datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z") == datetime("2023-08-02T14:00+02:00")   // true
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z"), datetime("2023-08-02T14:00+02:00")).dedup().count().next()   // 1
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T14:00+02:00")).is(P.gt(datetime("2023-08-02T11:00Z"))).count().next()   // 1

Of two values with the same instant and different offsets the first one met is kept (dedup(), a group() key); their order in a sort is unspecified. To compare the wall clocks instead, convert first: as_local() gives the wall-clock localdatetime (Time Zones).

duration: field-wise equal, ordered by length

Two durations are equal when their months, days and microseconds are equal: P1M is not P30D, and P1D is not PT24H (a day in a time zone may have 23 or 25 hours). Sorting compares their length as PostgreSQL does for an interval, counting a month as 30 days and a day as 24 hours; equal lengths are ordered by months, then days, then microseconds:

duration("P1M") == duration("P30D")   // false
g.inject(duration("P1M"), duration("P30D"), duration("PT719H")).order().to_list()   // [PT719H, P30D, P1M]

The other types: by calendar and clock

A date, a localdatetime and a time compare by their calendar or clock value.

g.inject(time("10:00")).is(P.between(time("09:00"), time("17:00"))).count().next()   // 1
g.inject(date("2023-08-02")).is(P.within(date("2023-08-02"), date("2023-08-03"))).count().next()   // 1

Different types

Values of different types are never equal, and an ordering predicate between them does not match (no error): a date is not a datetime, and a date is never equal to a string, as a UUID is not. Convert one side first (Conversions).

g.inject(date("2023-08-02")).is(P.eq("2023-08-02")).count().next()   // 0
g.inject(date("2023-08-02")).is(P.lt(datetime("2024-01-01T00:00Z"))).count().next()   // 0
g.inject(date("2023-08-02")).as_date().is(P.lt(datetime("2024-01-01T00:00Z"))).count().next()   // 1

order() of a mixed stream puts the dates after the numbers and before the strings (TinkerPop's orderability places its date type there), in the order date, localdatetime, datetime, time, duration:

g.inject("x", 1, duration("P1D"), time("01:00"), datetime("2023-08-02T00:00Z"), date("2023-08-02")).order().to_list()

Property indexes

A property index on a key holding dates and times serves has() with these same rules: an equality or P.within reads the values equal to the operand (a datetime by its instant, a duration field by field), a range (P.gt, P.between, ...) reads the values of the operand's type in that range. The results are always the same as without the index.

g.create_index(#{label: "person", key: "joined"});
g.v().has("name", "marko").property("joined", datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).iterate();
g.v().has_label("person").has("joined", datetime("2023-08-02T14:00+02:00")).count().next()   // 1

Text Formats

Dates are read and written as ISO 8601 text (RFC 3339 for a datetime, with the RFC 9557 zone suffix). No locale formats, no two-digit years, no guessing: a text is read as a date only where a date is asked for (a constructor, a conversion step, a declared schema format, a typed value in a file).

Canonical output

Every value has one text, the one tables, JSON, GraphML, GraphSON and as_string() write. It is the text java.time writes, so other tools read it back:

TypeCanonical text
date2023-08-02; a year before 1 or after 9999 with its sign: -0044-03-15
time09:30:00; a fraction only when it is not zero, as milliseconds or microseconds: 09:30:00.500, 09:30:00.123456
localdatetime2023-08-02T09:30:00 (the date, T, the time)
datetime2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00; Z for a zero offset; an offset with seconds as +00:19:32
durationP1Y2M3DT4H5M6S: years and months from the months, days, then the time part; a zero part is left out, a zero duration is PT0S; a sign before P when every part is negative (-P1M2D), else a sign per part (P1M-2D)
time("09:30:00.1").as_string()   // "09:30:00.100"
datetime("2023-08-02 09:30+00:00").as_string()   // "2023-08-02T09:30:00Z"
duration("PT90M").as_string()   // "PT1H30M"
duration("P2W").as_string()   // "P14D"

A duration keeps its three fields as they are: PT36H stays PT36H (not P1DT12H), and weeks are read as 7 days. Years and months are one field, months: P1Y2M is 14 months.

What is read

TypeAccepted text
dateYYYY-MM-DD; a year before 1 with its sign (-0044-03-15)
timeHH:MM, HH:MM:SS, HH:MM:SS.f with 1 to 9 fraction digits (digits below the microsecond are cut off)
localdatetimea date, optionally followed by T (or t, or a space) and a time; a date alone is midnight
datetimea local date-time, then an offset (Z, +02:00, +0200, +02, +00:19:32) and/or a zone in brackets ([Europe/Berlin])
duration[+-]P[nY][nM][nW][nD][T[nH][nM][n[.f]S]], a sign per number allowed (P1M-2D), letters in either case
datetime("2023-08-02T09:30+0200")   // datetime("2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00")
datetime("2023-08-02T09:30[Europe/Berlin]")   // datetime("2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00")
datetime("2023-08-02T09:30:00.123456789Z")   // datetime("2023-08-02T09:30:00.123456Z")
date("10000-01-01")   // error: expected a four-digit year
duration("1 day")   // error: not an ISO 8601 duration

A datetime with only a zone is resolved in it (a wall-clock time the zone skips moves forward, one it repeats takes the earlier offset, see Time Zones); with an offset and a zone the offset must be the zone's at that instant.

Strict and lenient: a datetime without an offset

TinkerPop reads a date-time text without an offset as UTC (asDate("2023-08-02") is midnight UTC). Graphersal does that only where a query asks for a conversion:

  • lenient (no offset = UTC, a date alone = midnight UTC): the datetime() / DateTime() constructor and the conversion steps as_date() and as_date(GType.DATETIME);
  • strict (an offset or a zone is required): every place a text is stored as a datetime, namely a property declared "format": "date-time" in the schema, the formatMinimum/formatMaximum bounds, a typed gx:OffsetDateTime in GraphSON or a change set, a saved query argument declared as a date-time, and the playground's property editor.
datetime("2023-08-02T09:30")   // datetime("2023-08-02T09:30:00Z")
g.inject("2023-08-02").as_date().next()   // datetime("2023-08-02T00:00:00Z")

A stored instant without its offset would be a guess about where it was written; the strict rule turns that guess into an error that names the expected form. The other types have no offset, so they read the same everywhere.

Time Zones

A time zone is never stored in a value. A datetime carries a fixed UTC offset (the one it was written with); an operation that needs a zone takes it as an argument and gives back a datetime with the zone's offset at that instant. This is the PostgreSQL model (AT TIME ZONE, a session zone for the calendar arithmetic), with the zone passed explicitly instead of a session setting.

Zone arguments

A zone argument is one of:

  • an IANA zone name: "Europe/Berlin", "America/New_York", "UTC";
  • a fixed offset: "+02:00", "-0530", "Z".

The IANA rules come from the time zone database bundled with Graphersal (the jiff-tzdb crate). Every machine, and the browser playground, gives the same answer to the same query, and a replayed journal computes what it computed when it was written; the database changes only with a Graphersal release, not with an operating system update. An unknown name is an error, found before any value is read:

g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).at_zone("Mars/Olympus").next()   // error: unknown time zone

The steps that take a zone: at_zone(zone), as_local(zone), date_add(.., zone), date_diff(.., zone), age(.., zone), date_trunc(.., zone), date_part(.., zone), and today(zone). Only a datetime (and the localdatetime of at_zone) takes one; the other types have no instant, and a zone argument for them is an error.

Moving between a datetime and its wall clock

  • at_zone(zone) on a datetime: the same instant, written with the zone's offset at it (PostgreSQL AT TIME ZONE, java.time atZoneSameInstant).
  • at_zone(zone) on a localdatetime: the wall-clock time read in the zone, the datetime of that instant (java.time atZone).
  • as_local() / as_local(zone): the wall-clock localdatetime a datetime shows on its own offset or in the zone (toLocalDateTime).
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).at_zone("America/New_York").next()   // datetime("2023-08-02T08:00:00-04:00")
g.inject(localdatetime("2023-08-02T12:00")).at_zone("+02:00").next()   // datetime("2023-08-02T12:00:00+02:00")
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).as_local("Asia/Tokyo").next()   // localdatetime("2023-08-02T21:00:00")

Daylight saving: gaps and folds

Where a zone moves its clocks, a wall-clock time can be missing (a spring-forward gap) or happen twice (a fall-back fold). Graphersal resolves both as PostgreSQL and java.time do (the "compatible" rule), never with an error:

  • a time in a gap moves forward by the length of the gap: 02:30 on 2023-03-26 in Berlin becomes 03:30+02:00;
  • a time in a fold takes the earlier offset: 02:30 on 2023-10-29 in Berlin is 02:30+02:00, the first of the two.
g.inject(localdatetime("2023-03-26T02:30")).at_zone("Europe/Berlin").next()   // datetime("2023-03-26T03:30:00+02:00")
g.inject(localdatetime("2023-10-29T02:30")).at_zone("Europe/Berlin").next()   // datetime("2023-10-29T02:30:00+02:00")

The same rule applies to a text with only a zone (datetime("2023-03-26T02:30[Europe/Berlin]")) and to every result a zone computes on the wall clock.

Calendar arithmetic in a zone

Without a zone a datetime is computed on its own fixed offset: date_add(DT.day, 1) adds 24 hours, as TinkerPop specifies. With a zone, calendar units work on the zone's wall clock, so a day stays a calendar day across a daylight saving change (23 or 25 hours long), while hours stay hours:

g.inject(datetime("2023-03-25T12:00+01:00")).date_add(DT.day, 1).next()   // datetime("2023-03-26T12:00:00+01:00")
g.inject(datetime("2023-03-25T12:00+01:00")).date_add(DT.day, 1, "Europe/Berlin").next()   // datetime("2023-03-26T12:00:00+02:00")
g.inject(datetime("2023-03-25T12:00+01:00")).date_add(DT.hour, 24, "Europe/Berlin").next()   // datetime("2023-03-26T13:00:00+02:00")

The same holds for date_diff() in days and larger units, age(), date_trunc() and date_part(): they read the wall clock of the zone. Without a zone, date_diff() and age() read both operands on the wall clock of the second operand's offset:

g.inject(datetime("2023-03-26T12:00+02:00")).date_diff(datetime("2023-03-25T12:00+01:00"), DT.day).next()   // 0 (23 hours)
g.inject(datetime("2023-03-26T12:00+02:00")).date_diff(datetime("2023-03-25T12:00+01:00"), DT.day, "Europe/Berlin").next()   // 1
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).date_trunc(DT.day, "America/New_York").next()   // datetime("2023-08-02T00:00:00-04:00")

Arithmetic

Three steps compute with dates: date_add() moves a value, date_diff() measures the distance between two values as a number, age() as a duration. All of them are checked: a result outside the years -9999 to 9999 is an error, never a wrapped value. In a script the operators + and - do the same (script values).

Units: the DT token

DT.second, DT.minute, DT.hour and DT.day are TinkerPop's (the bare names second, minute, hour and day work too, as in the TinkerPop scenarios). Graphersal adds the smaller and the calendar units, with PostgreSQL's field names:

UnitKindAdding it
DT.microsecond, DT.millisecond, DT.second, DT.minute, DT.houra fixed lengthmoves the instant (or the clock) by that many microseconds
DT.day, DT.weekcalendar daysmoves the wall-clock date; in a zone the time of day is kept across a daylight saving change
DT.month, DT.quarter, DT.year, DT.decade, DT.century, DT.millenniumcalendar months (1, 3, 12, 120, 1200, 12000)moves the month and clamps the day to the end of the target month

DT.day_of_week, DT.iso_day_of_week, DT.day_of_year, DT.iso_year, DT.epoch and DT.offset are parts, not units: only date_part() takes them.

date_add()

date_add(DT.unit, n) adds n units (a negative n subtracts); date_add(duration) adds a duration. Both take an optional zone as the last argument (Time Zones).

g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).date_add(DT.hour, 36).next()   // datetime("2023-08-04T00:00:00Z")
g.inject(date("2023-08-02")).date_add(day, 3).next()   // date("2023-08-05")
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).date_add(DT.millisecond, 1500).next()   // datetime("2023-08-02T12:00:01.500Z")

Month ends. Adding months keeps the day of the month where it exists and otherwise takes the last day of the target month, as PostgreSQL and java.time do. Each step clamps on its own, so two single months can end earlier than two months at once:

g.inject(date("2024-01-31")).date_add(DT.month, 1).next()   // date("2024-02-29")
g.inject(date("2024-01-31")).date_add(DT.month, 2).next()   // date("2024-03-31")
g.inject(date("2024-01-31")).date_add(DT.month, 1).date_add(DT.month, 1).next()   // date("2024-03-29")

A duration is added in PostgreSQL's order: its months first (clamped), then its days, then its time part.

g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).date_add(duration("P1M1DT1H")).next()   // datetime("2023-09-03T13:00:00Z")
g.inject(date("2024-02-29")).date_add(duration("P1Y1D")).next()   // date("2025-03-01")

What each type accepts:

TypeDT unitsA duration
datetimeall units; a fixed length moves the instant and keeps the offset (TinkerPop: a day is 24 hours at a fixed offset), with a zone the result takes the zone's offsetany
localdatetimeall units, on the wall clockany
dateday and largerwithout a time part
timehour and smaller; the clock wraps around midnight (PostgreSQL time + interval)without months or days
durationall units: adds to the matching fieldany (field by field)
g.inject(time("23:00")).date_add(DT.hour, 2).next()   // time("01:00:00")
g.inject(date("2024-02-29")).date_add(DT.hour, 2).next()   // error: adding the unit hour is not defined for a date

date_diff()

date_diff(other) is TinkerPop's dateDiff(): the incoming value minus other in milliseconds, an int64, each operand's epoch milliseconds rounded down. other is a value or a child traversal whose first result is the operand; () (null) stands for the epoch.

g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).date_diff(datetime("2023-08-01T00:00Z")).next()   // 129600000
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).date_diff(__.constant(datetime("2023-08-01T00:00Z"))).next()   // 129600000
g.inject(datetime("1970-01-01T00:00:01Z")).date_diff(()).next()   // 1000

Graphersal extends it to the other types (both operands of one type: a date counts from midnight, a time within the day; () is 1970-01-01 or midnight) and adds date_diff(other, DT.unit[, zone]): the difference in whole units, truncated toward zero.

  • Units below a day count the elapsed time.
  • Days and weeks count wall-clock days (a datetime on the wall clock of other's offset, or of the zone).
  • Months and larger count as java.time's ChronoUnit.between: a month is complete when the day of the month (and the time) is reached again, so January 31 to February 28 is 0 months.
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T12:00Z")).date_diff(datetime("2023-08-01T00:00Z"), DT.hour).next()   // 36
g.inject(time("10:00")).date_diff(time("09:00"), DT.minute).next()   // 60
g.inject(date("2024-02-28")).date_diff(date("2024-01-31"), DT.month).next()   // 0
g.inject(date("2024-03-31")).date_diff(date("2024-02-29"), DT.month).next()   // 1

age()

age(other[, zone]) is PostgreSQL's age: the difference as a duration of whole years and months, days and a time part, all with the same sign. It is counted down from the incoming value to other with PostgreSQL's borrowing rules, so swapping the operands negates the result. Both operands have the same type; () is an error.

g.inject(date("2001-04-10")).age(date("1957-06-13")).next()   // duration("P43Y9M27D")
g.inject(date("1957-06-13")).age(date("2001-04-10")).next()   // duration("-P43Y9M27D")
g.inject(datetime("2024-02-29T00:00Z")).age(datetime("2023-01-31T12:00Z")).next()   // duration("P1Y28DT12H")

To get a plain number of days, years or hours, use date_diff(other, DT.unit); to get a duration of elapsed time without calendar units, subtract the two values in a script (a - b).

Truncation and Parts

date_trunc(DT.unit) is PostgreSQL's date_trunc, and date_part(DT.unit) is its extract. Both are Graphersal extensions; TinkerPop has neither. A datetime is read on its own wall clock, or on the wall clock of a zone given as the last argument (Time Zones).

date_trunc()

The fields below the unit become their first value: the start of the hour, the day, the month. A truncated datetime keeps its offset (or, with a zone, takes the zone's offset at the new instant).

g.inject(datetime("2023-08-17T15:47:12.5+02:00")).date_trunc(DT.hour).next()   // datetime("2023-08-17T15:00:00+02:00")
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-17T15:47:12.5+02:00")).date_trunc(DT.week).next()   // datetime("2023-08-14T00:00:00+02:00")
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-17T15:47:12.5+02:00")).date_trunc(DT.day, "UTC").next()   // datetime("2023-08-17T00:00:00Z")
g.inject(date("2023-08-17")).date_trunc(DT.quarter).next()   // date("2023-07-01")
g.inject(duration("P1Y2M3DT4H5M")).date_trunc(DT.day).next()   // duration("P1Y2M3D")
UnitTruncates to
microsecond ... hourthe start of that unit of the clock
daymidnight
weekMonday, midnight (ISO 8601 weeks)
month, quarter, yearthe first day of the month, of the quarter (January, April, July, October), of the year
decadethe first day of a year divisible by 10 (2020-01-01)
century, millenniumthe first day of a year ending in 01/001: centuries and millennia start at year 1, as PostgreSQL counts them (2001-01-01 starts the 21st century)

A date takes day and larger, a time hour and smaller, a duration keeps the fields at and above the unit (month and larger keep whole multiples of the unit's months and drop the days and the time part).

date_part()

One field as a number: an int64, except DT.epoch, a float64 of seconds.

PartValue
DT.year, DT.month (1-12), DT.day (1-31), DT.hour, DT.minute, DT.second (0-59)the field
DT.millisecond (0-999), DT.microsecond (0-999999)the fraction of the second; unlike PostgreSQL, not the seconds with the fraction
DT.quarter (1-4)the quarter
DT.week (1-53)the ISO 8601 week number
DT.iso_yearthe ISO 8601 week-numbering year (2023-01-01 is in week 52 of 2022)
DT.day_of_week0 = Sunday to 6 = Saturday (PostgreSQL dow)
DT.iso_day_of_week1 = Monday to 7 = Sunday (PostgreSQL isodow)
DT.day_of_year (1-366)the day of the year
DT.decade, DT.century, DT.millenniumas PostgreSQL counts them (the 21st century is 2001-2100)
DT.epochseconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z (a localdatetime read as UTC); for a duration its length with a year of 365.25 days and a month of 30 days
DT.offsetthe UTC offset of a datetime in seconds
g.inject(date("2023-08-17")).date_part(DT.day_of_week).next()   // 4
g.inject(datetime("2023-01-01T15:47:12.5+02:00")).date_part(DT.week).next()   // 52
g.inject(datetime("2023-01-01T15:47:12.5+02:00")).date_part(DT.iso_year).next()   // 2022
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-17T15:47:12.5+02:00")).date_part(DT.epoch).next()   // 1692280032.5
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-17T15:47:12.5+02:00")).date_part(DT.offset).next()   // 7200
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T02:00Z")).date_part(DT.day, "America/New_York").next()   // 1

A date has no clock parts (hour and smaller), a time only those (and epoch, the seconds since midnight). A duration gives PostgreSQL's interval fields: year and month from its months (14 months are 1 year and 2 months), day its days, hour and smaller from its time part; it has no week, day-of parts, iso_year or offset:

g.inject(duration("P1Y2M3DT4H5M6.5S")).date_part(DT.month).next()   // 2
g.inject(date("2023-08-17")).date_part(DT.hour).next()   // error: the part hour is not defined for a date

Conversions

A value becomes a date only through an explicit step; nothing is converted by guessing (a string that looks like a date stays a string).

as_date(): TinkerPop's asDate()

as_date() converts to a datetime exactly as TinkerPop's asDate() does:

IncomingResult
a datetimeunchanged
a stringread leniently as ISO 8601 / RFC 3339: without an offset it is UTC, a date alone is midnight UTC (Text Formats)
an int64milliseconds since the epoch, in UTC
a date, a localdatetimethe datetime at UTC (Graphersal: TinkerPop has no such types)
anything else (a float64, (), a list, a map, a time, a duration, an element)an error starting with "Can't parse", as in TinkerPop
g.inject("2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00", 1690000000000, date("2023-08-02")).as_date().to_list()   // [2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00, 2023-07-22T04:26:40Z, 2023-08-02T00:00:00Z]
g.inject(1.5).as_date().next()   // error: Can't parse float64 1.5 as a datetime

as_date(GType.X): to another date type

as_date(GType.DATETIME | DATE | LOCALDATETIME | TIME) converts to that type (a Graphersal extension, spelled like as_number(GType.LONG)):

Incoming →DATETIMEDATELOCALDATETIMETIME
stringlenient, as as_date()strict: a date textstrict: a local date-time textstrict: a time text
datetimeunchangedits wall-clock date (at its own offset)its wall clockits wall-clock time
localdatetimeat UTCits dateunchangedits time
datemidnight UTCunchangedmidnightan error
timean erroran erroran errorunchanged
int64epoch milliseconds, UTCan erroran erroran error

GType.DURATION is not a target here: use as_duration(). To read a datetime's wall clock in another zone, use as_local(zone) first (Time Zones).

g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T23:30-07:00")).as_date(GType.DATE).next()   // date("2023-08-02")
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T23:30-07:00")).as_local("UTC").as_date(GType.DATE).next()   // date("2023-08-03")
g.inject("2023-08-02").as_date(GType.DATE).next()   // date("2023-08-02")
g.inject("2023-08-02T09:30").as_date(GType.DATE).next()   // error: unexpected text after the value

as_duration()

as_duration() reads an ISO 8601 duration text; a duration passes unchanged, anything else fails with "Can't parse".

g.inject("PT90M").as_duration().next()   // duration("PT1H30M")

To numbers and text

  • as_number() of a datetime is its epoch milliseconds (TinkerPop), rounded down; the other date types are not numbers (use date_part(DT.epoch) or date_diff()).
  • as_string() of any date is its canonical text; in a script, x.as_string() does the same.
  • cast(GType.DATETIME) (and the other date tokens) parses a string or, for DATETIME, reads an int64 as epoch milliseconds, like as_date(GType.X).
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T00:00Z")).as_number().next()   // 1690934400000
g.inject(datetime("2023-08-02T09:30+02:00")).as_string().next()   // "2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00"
g.inject(date("2023-08-02")).as_number().next()   // error: Cast exception

Storing text as a date

A property written as a string stays a string. To store dates, declare the property in the schema ("format": "date-time"): in open and closed mode a string written to it is converted on write. Or convert in the query: property("at", __.constant(text).as_date()), or write a date value (property("on", date("2023-08-02"))).

now() and today()

now() is the current time as a datetime in UTC; today() is its date, and today(zone) the date in a zone (an IANA name or an offset).

type_of(now())   // "datetime"
now() == now()   // true
type_of(today("Europe/Berlin"))   // "date"
g.add_v("event").property("at", now()).values("at").count().next()   // 1

The start of the evaluation

Like PostgreSQL's now() (CURRENT_TIMESTAMP), now() is the time the script evaluation started, the same value for every call in it: a script that stamps a thousand elements stamps them all with one instant, and now() == now() holds. In the playground a whole script is one unit, so now() is the start of that unit. A saved query called from a script sees its caller's now().

now() and today() are script functions, evaluated before the traversal runs: the traversal gets the resulting value as a constant (inject(now()), property("at", now()), has("at", P.lt(now()))). The journal of a Store and a change set record that value, never the call, so a replay or a recovery writes the same instant, not the time of the replay.

today() is the date of now() in UTC, PostgreSQL's current_date in a UTC session. For the date in another zone pass the zone, or convert the instant yourself:

today("UTC") == today()   // true
g.inject(now()).as_local("America/Los_Angeles").as_date(GType.DATE).next() == today("America/Los_Angeles")   // true

Pinning the clock (hosts)

A host that needs a deterministic clock (tests, a replay of a recorded session) pins it on its engine with graphersal::script::pin_now; every evaluation on that engine then returns the pinned instant, until it is unpinned with None:

use graphersal::script::{engine_with_options, pin_now};
use graphersal::temporal::DateTime;

let mut engine = engine_with_options(&limits, authorizer, &presets);
pin_now(&mut engine, Some("2023-08-02T23:30:00-07:00".parse::<DateTime>()?));
// now() is 2023-08-02T23:30:00-07:00, today() is 2023-08-03 (the UTC date)
pin_now(&mut engine, None); // the system clock again

The system clock is read through web_time, so now() works the same in the WebAssembly playground.

Dates in a Schema

A schema declares a date property as a JSON Schema string with a format, and bounds it with the format* keywords. The full reference (every keyword, the errors and why, inference and diffs) is on the Schemas page; this page is the overview.

formatTypeExample value
date-timedatetime2024-05-01T09:30:00+02:00
local-date-timelocaldatetime2024-05-01T09:30:00 (a Graphersal name: JSON Schema has none)
datedate2024-05-01
timetime09:30:00 (local; JSON Schema's own time requires an offset)
durationdurationP1Y2M3DT4H

JSON Schema validators treat format as an annotation and ignore one they do not know, so a schema with these formats stays usable with other tools; Pydantic writes date-time, date, time and duration for datetime, date, time and timedelta fields.

Coercion on write

In open and closed mode a string written to a declared date property becomes the date: the declaration says the property is a date, so nothing is guessed. The text must be one the type reads (Text Formats); a date-time text needs its UTC offset or a zone (2024-05-01T09:30 is refused, never read as UTC). A date value is stored as it is; a value of another date type is refused (a date is not a datetime). Reads never convert: a string stored before the schema was set does not conform to the format, and set_schema reports it.

g.set_schema(#{vertices: #{event: #{schema: #{type: "object", properties: #{
    at: #{type: "string", format: "date-time"},
    on: #{type: "string", format: "date", formatMinimum: "2000-01-01"}
}}}}}, SchemaMode.open);
g.add_v("event").property("at", "2024-05-01T09:30:00+02:00").property("on", date("2024-05-01")).iterate();
g.v().has_label("event").values("at").next().offset   // 7200: a datetime, not a string

{
    g.set_schema(#{vertices: #{event: #{schema: #{type: "object", properties: #{
        at: #{type: "string", format: "date-time"}
    }}}}}, SchemaMode.open);
    g.add_v("event").property("at", "2024-05-01T09:30").iterate()
}   // refused: the text has no offset

Bounds

formatMinimum, formatMaximum, formatExclusiveMinimum and formatExclusiveMaximum (the keywords of JSON Schema's format-comparison proposal, which ajv-formats implements) bound a date property. Their value is the text of a value of the node's type, and a value is compared as the type compares: a datetime by its instant, a duration by its length. minimum and maximum stay number keywords.

{ "type": "string", "format": "date-time", "formatMinimum": "2020-01-01T00:00:00Z" }
{ "type": "string", "format": "duration", "formatExclusiveMaximum": "P1D" }

Inference

infer_schema() reports a stored date with its format ({"type": "string", "format": "date-time"}), and a position that holds strings and dates as an anyOf, so freezing the structure you have (g.set_schema(g.infer_schema(), SchemaMode.closed)) keeps the dates dates. The playground's schema editor offers the five formats as types and their bounds as constraints.

Storage and Exchange

A date keeps its type wherever it goes: in memory, in a snapshot or a Store, in a change set and in a GraphSON file. GraphML has no date type and needs the schema.

In memory

A date is stored inline in the property value, 16 bytes at most, without a heap allocation: a date is a day number, a time and a localdatetime microseconds, a datetime microseconds since the epoch plus its offset in seconds, a duration its months, days and microseconds. Equality and ordering compare these numbers (Comparing and Sorting).

Snapshots, journals and the Store

The binary format (packed snapshots .gsnap, Store segments, the write-ahead log) has a value tag per type, 9 to 13, defined in the format specification: the exact payload, the range of each type, and the rule that a datetime keeps its offset while equality uses the instant. These tags came with file format version 2: a build that knows them writes version 2 and reads versions 1 and 2, so a .gsnap written by 0.1.x still loads, while an older build refuses a version 2 file instead of misreading it. See Format Versions and Upgrade for a Store written by 0.1.x.

Change sets

A serialized ChangeSet (feature serde) writes a date as a per-value type tag in TinkerPop's GraphSON style, so a replay restores the type without a schema:

TypeTag
datetime{"@type": "gx:OffsetDateTime", "@value": "2024-05-01T09:30:00+02:00"}
date, localdatetime, timegx:LocalDate, gx:LocalDateTime, gx:LocalTime
duration of microseconds onlygx:Duration (PT26H)
duration of months and days onlygx:Period (P1Y2M3D)
any other durationgraphersal:Interval (P1MT2H)

Reading is strict: the text must be a value of the tag's type, and a gx:OffsetDateTime must carry its offset.

GraphSON

GraphSON 3.0 reads and writes the java.time types: g:Date/g:Timestamp (epoch milliseconds) become a datetime in UTC, gx:OffsetDateTime, gx:Instant and gx:ZonedDateTime a datetime with the offset of the text (the zone id of a gx:ZonedDateTime is dropped and reported), gx:LocalDate, gx:LocalDateTime and gx:LocalTime the local types, gx:Duration and gx:Period a duration. The export writes the tags of the change set table above, which TinkerGraph's g.io(file).read() loads, with one exception: a duration with both months or days and a time part has no java.time type, so it is written as graphersal:Interval, which only Graphersal reads (a deliberate deviation). Digits below a microsecond are cut and reported, and the java.time types Graphersal cannot hold (gx:Year, gx:YearMonth, gx:MonthDay, gx:OffsetTime, gx:ZoneOffset) are skipped and reported. The full mapping is on the GraphSON page.

A date-like string without a type tag (GraphSON 1.0, types=false) stays a string; declare the property in the schema to store it as a date.

GraphML

GraphML has no date type: a date is written as its canonical text under a string key. It is read back as a date only when the target graph's schema declares the property with a date format: set the schema on the empty graph first, then import (the playground's "Load from file" takes the schema file next to the graph file; the CLI's --schema). Without a schema the text stays a string. See UUID Values, which describes the same rule for UUIDs, and the Schemas page.

JSON, tables and the playground

Tables, JSON results, the CLI's visualizers, MCP and the dev server write the canonical text ("2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00"); a script value prints as its literal (datetime("2023-08-02T09:30:00+02:00")). The playground's property editor keeps the type: it shows and edits a date property as one of the five date types (Text Formats).

From Python

The Python binding converts the five types to and from the standard datetime module, both as results and as params=, to the microsecond (the resolution of both sides):

GraphersalPython
datetimeaware datetime.datetime with tzinfo=datetime.timezone(timedelta(seconds=offset))
localdatetimenaive datetime.datetime
datedatetime.date
timenaive datetime.time
duration without monthsdatetime.timedelta
duration with monthsgraphersal.Interval(months, days, micros)
import datetime as dt
import graphersal

graph = graphersal.Graph()
at = dt.datetime(2023, 8, 2, 9, 30, tzinfo=dt.timezone(dt.timedelta(hours=2)))
graph.query("g.inject(x).date_add(DT.day, 1).next()", params={"x": at})
# datetime.datetime(2023, 8, 3, 9, 30, tzinfo=datetime.timezone(datetime.timedelta(seconds=7200)))
graph.query('duration("P1Y2M")')
# Interval('P1Y2M')
  • An aware datetime with any tzinfo (a zoneinfo.ZoneInfo too) is passed with the UTC offset it has at that instant; the zone name is not kept. An offset with a fraction of a second is refused.
  • An aware datetime.time is refused: a time of day has no instant without a date.
  • A timedelta becomes whole days and the rest, both with the sign of the whole (timedelta(hours=-1) is -PT1H).
  • graphersal.Interval is immutable, equal when its three fields are equal (Interval("P1M") != Interval(0, 30), as in the engine), has months, days, micros and to_iso(), and is built from the fields or from ISO 8601 text (Interval("P1Y2M3DT4H")).
  • Python's datetime holds the years 1 to 9999; a date before year 1 cannot be returned as one (read it with as_string()).

The binding's README has the details and more examples.

TinkerPop Compatibility

TinkerPop 3.8 has one date type, datetime (a Java OffsetDateTime), the literal datetime(..), the steps asDate(), dateAdd() and dateDiff(), the units DT.second, DT.minute, DT.hour and DT.day, and the tokens GType.DATETIME and GType.DURATION (a Java Duration, which no TinkerPop step produces). Graphersal implements all of it as TinkerPop specifies, with no deviation:

  • datetime("..") (also spelled DateTime("..")) reads ISO 8601 text, a text without an offset as UTC;
  • asDate() converts text and epoch milliseconds, and fails with "Can't parse" for the same inputs as TinkerPop;
  • dateAdd(DT.unit, n) keeps the offset and moves the instant, a day being 24 hours;
  • dateDiff(other) is the difference in milliseconds, null being the epoch;
  • asNumber() of a datetime is its epoch milliseconds;
  • equality and ordering use the instant ("Dates are evaluated based on the numerical comparison of Unix Epoch time"), and dates sort after numbers and before strings.

Every date scenario of the vendored TinkerPop 3.8.2 suite passes (DateTime, AsDate, DateAdd, DateDiff, the date cases of TypeOf and AsNumber), except two Orderability scenarios that also hold a set literal ({"x", "y", "z"}), for which Graphersal has no value type (TinkerPop Compliance).

Extensions

Everything else on the pages of this part is a Graphersal extension, modelled on PostgreSQL:

  • the types date, localdatetime and time (GType.DATE, LOCALDATETIME, TIME; typeOf names LocalDate, LocalDateTime, LocalTime), and duration as a value with months, days and microseconds (PostgreSQL's interval, broader than Java's Duration), with their constructors;
  • the units DT.microsecond, DT.millisecond, DT.week to DT.millennium and the parts DT.day_of_week, DT.iso_day_of_week, DT.day_of_year, DT.iso_year, DT.epoch, DT.offset;
  • date_add(duration), zone arguments, date_diff(other, DT.unit), age(), date_trunc(), date_part(), at_zone(), as_local(), as_duration(), as_date(GType.X);
  • now(), today(), the getters and operators of script values;
  • the schema formats and bounds, GraphSON's java.time types beyond g:Date, and the Python mapping.

The extensions add behaviour where TinkerPop defines none; none of them changes what a TinkerPop step returns. The one deliberate difference in the exchange formats is GraphSON's graphersal:Interval for a duration that no java.time type can hold (Storage and Exchange); all deviations are listed on TinkerPop Deviations.

Schemas

A graph can store a schema: which vertex and edge labels exist, which properties they carry, of which types and within which constraints, and how edges may connect labels. The schema is plain data in one format, the same in Rust, the script DSL, Python and the playground: our envelope outside, standard JSON Schema 2020-12 inside (a strict subset), so a model_json_schema() from Pydantic can be pasted as a label's schema.

The rule behind enforcement: the storage owns consistency. Every operation that changes the graph passes the schema inside one storage call, never in a step, and every traversal is one unit of work: it is applied completely or not at all.

A first schema

g.set_schema(`{
  "mode": "closed",
  "vertices": {
    "person": {"schema": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "name": {"type": "string", "minLength": 1},
        "age":  {"type": ["integer", "null"], "minimum": 0}
      },
      "required": ["name"]
    }}
  },
  "edges": {
    "knows": {"connections": [{"from": "person", "to": "person"}],
              "schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"weight": {"type": "number"}}}}
  }
}`)
g.add_v("person").property("name", "Ann").next()     // ok
g.add_v("person").property("age", -1).next()         // error: age >= 0 (and name is required)

g.get_schema() returns the stored schema as a map (() without one), g.infer_schema() the schema the data satisfies. Rendered as the final value of a session (the CLI, the playground) a schema shows as a table; --format mermaid|plantuml|json|jsonschema|markdown|tree picks another view.

Freeze the structure you have

A common way to start: build the graph without a schema, experiment until the shape is right, then freeze that shape so every later write has to follow it:

g.set_schema(g.infer_schema(), SchemaMode.closed)   // or SchemaMode.open / SchemaMode.none

set_schema(schema, mode) stores schema with its mode replaced by mode (an inferred schema has mode none, which enforces nothing). The mode is a SchemaMode token (SchemaMode.closed, SchemaMode::closed) or one of the strings "none", "open", "closed"; validate_schema(schema, mode) is the dry run. SchemaMode is a reserved name in the script scope.

BindingFreeze
DSLg.set_schema(g.infer_schema(), SchemaMode.closed) (also setSchema(.., "closed"))
Rustlet s = g.infer_schema()?.with_mode(SchemaMode::Closed); g_mut.set_schema(s)?
Pythongraph.set_schema(graph.infer_schema(), mode="closed")
PlaygroundSchema panel: Freeze as open / Freeze as closed (shown while the graph stores no enforcing schema)

What each mode freezes:

  • open: the labels and properties that exist get their types and required lists; new labels and new properties stay allowed (unchecked).
  • closed: additionally, no other label, no other property (at any depth) and no edge between other labels than the ones that exist.

It always succeeds on the data the schema was inferred from, in both modes: inference declares every kind seen at every position and requires only the keys every element has (see Inference). The one exception is closed with elements without a label: an unlabeled vertex or edge has no label to declare, and a closed schema admits only declared labels. Then the call fails, changes nothing, and the report names them:

Cannot apply the Closed schema: the existing data violates it (2 kinds of violations on 2 elements of 6 checked)
  1) 1 edge without a label (Closed admits only declared labels) [ids: "7"]
  2) 1 vertex without a label (Closed admits only declared labels) [ids: "3"]

Freeze such a graph in open mode (it admits unlabeled elements unchecked), or give those elements a label first with the label steps (add_label, drop_label, set_label) and freeze again:

g.v("3").add_label("thing").to_list();                                  // a vertex from the report
g.e().not(__.has_label()).set_label("link").to_list();   // every unlabeled edge
g.set_schema(g.infer_schema(), SchemaMode.closed)

(g.v().not(__.has_label()).add_label("thing") labels every unlabeled vertex; Rust: the same steps, or GraphStorage::add_vertex_label/set_edge_label.) (The generated large sample graph has unlabeled edges: it freezes open, not closed.)

Later changes go through patch_schema (add a property, relax a rule) like any other schema.

The format

Envelope

KeyTypeMeaning
$schemastring, optionalThe format: https://graphersal.dev/schema/v1 (any other value is an error).
metaobject, optionalFree-form data the library stores, round-trips and never interprets (a version, a status, server data). Changing it is a schema change.
mode"none" | "open" | "closed", default "none"What is enforced, see Modes.
verticesobjectVertex label → {"schema": <label schema>}.
edgesobjectEdge label → {"connections": [{"from": .., "to": ..}], "schema": <label schema>}.

A label schema is a JSON Schema object node describing the element's property map: {"type": "object", "properties": {..}, "required": [..], "additionalProperties": ..} plus annotations. It may carry $defs (for $ref), $schema and $id (accepted and not stored). A label without schema declares no properties. A connection's from/to is a vertex label or * (any label).

Unknown keys are errors everywhere, the envelope included: {"mdoe": "closed"} is rejected with its location (Invalid schema at /mdoe: unknown key 'mdoe'), never silently ignored.

The canonical form (what get_schema, to_json and every binding return) always writes $schema, mode, vertices and edges, keywords in a fixed order, integers as integers. The empty schema (mode none, no meta, no labels) is no schema: set_schema({}) removes the stored schema. The format is described by the meta-schema graphersal-schema-v1.json (graphersal::schema::META_SCHEMA_JSON).

Types

JSON SchemaEngine typeNote
"integer"int64A value outside i64 cannot be stored at all; 3.0 is not an integer.
"number"float64An int64 written to it is coerced when exactly representable; a stored int64 does not conform.
"string"string
"string" + "format": "uuid"uuidA canonical UUID string is coerced on write; a stored string does not conform.
"string" + "format": "date-time"datetimeAn instant with its UTC offset (2024-05-01T09:30:00+02:00).
"string" + "format": "date"dateA calendar day (2024-05-01).
"string" + "format": "local-date-time"localdatetimeA date and time without a zone (2024-05-01T09:30:00). A Graphersal format name: JSON Schema has none.
"string" + "format": "time"timeA time of day without an offset (09:30:00). JSON Schema's own time requires an offset; Graphersal's is local.
"string" + "format": "duration"durationISO 8601 (P1Y2M3DT4H): months, days and microseconds.
"boolean", "null"boolean, null
"array" + itemsarray<T>items is a full schema (constraints and nullability apply to the items); without items any item.
"array" + "format": "vector" (+ element, dimension, metric)vector<f32, 768>A vector of the declared element (f32 default, f16, i8, bit) and dimension (optional). A list of numbers is coerced on write, a vector of another element quantized; a stored list does not conform. items is not allowed next to it; metric is an annotation. Book page Vectors.
"object" + propertiesobjectWith required and additionalProperties.
["integer", "null"]union<int64|null>A type array: any of the listed types.
anyOf: [..]union<..>At least one member accepts the value (Pydantic's Optional[X] is anyOf: [X, {"type": "null"}]).
{} (no type)anyAdmits every value.

Diagnostics, Display and GType keep the engine's names (int64, float64, uuid, datetime, localdatetime, ...).

Dates and times. In open and closed mode a property declared with a temporal format coerces a string on write: any text the type's parser accepts (ISO 8601 / RFC 3339; the canonical form and the usual variants such as 2024-05-01 09:30Z or 09:30) becomes the temporal value, and text it refuses is a coercion failure that names the expected form. A date-time text must carry its UTC offset or a time zone (2024-05-01T09:30:00Z, 2024-05-01T09:30[Europe/Berlin]): 2024-05-01T09:30 is refused, never read as UTC, and the same holds for a formatMinimum/formatMaximum bound and a typed gx:OffsetDateTime (only the explicit conversion step as_date() keeps TinkerPop's "no offset is UTC"). This is the explicit declaration at work, like the uuid coercion, never a guess from content: an undeclared date-like string stays a string. A stored string does not conform to a temporal format (reads never coerce), and one temporal type never conforms to another (a date is not a datetime). JSON Schema's format is an annotation for other validators, which ignore a format they do not know, so a schema with local-date-time stays usable with them. The part Dates and Times describes the types themselves; its page Dates in a Schema has examples.

Keywords

KindKeywords
Structuretype, format (uuid, date-time, date, local-date-time, time, duration on a string; vector on an array), element, dimension, metric (with format: "vector"), items, properties, required, additionalProperties (true/false), anyOf
Constraintsminimum, maximum, exclusiveMinimum, exclusiveMaximum (numbers), formatMinimum, formatMaximum, formatExclusiveMinimum, formatExclusiveMaximum (dates and times), minLength, maxLength, pattern (strings), minItems, maxItems (arrays), enum, const (any value)
Annotations (no effect on validation)title, description, $comment, examples, deprecated
Create-time defaults (Defaults on create)default (also an annotation below the top level), defaultFunction (uuidv4, uuidv7, now, today)
References$ref: "#/$defs/Name" with $defs at the label schema's root; inlined when the schema is loaded

A constraint applies to the values of its own kind and ignores the others (JSON Schema semantics): in {"type": ["integer", "string"], "minimum": 10, "minLength": 3} the bound checks the integers and the length the strings. Next to a declared type, a keyword of another kind is an error (minLength on an integer is a mistake, not a no-op). enum/const compare JSON values (1 equals 1.0, a uuid and a date or time compare as their canonical text, so a datetime matches only the text with its own offset).

formatMinimum, formatMaximum, formatExclusiveMinimum and formatExclusiveMaximum bound a date or time: the keywords of JSON Schema's format-comparison proposal (ajv-formats implements them; other validators ignore unknown keywords). Their value is the text of a value of the node's temporal format, and they are valid only next to one (minimum stays a number keyword):

{ "type": "string", "format": "date-time", "formatMinimum": "2020-01-01T00:00:00Z" }
{ "type": "string", "format": "duration", "formatExclusiveMaximum": "P1D" }

A value is compared with its type's ordering: a datetime by its instant (2020-01-01T01:00:00+01:00 equals the minimum above), a duration by its length (a month counts 30 days, a day 24 hours, as PostgreSQL orders intervals), the others by their calendar or clock value.

Local references are inlined: a loaded schema has no $ref/$defs, and a reference cycle is an error (recursive schemas are not supported). Only annotations, default and defaultFunction may sit next to a $ref; they override the definition's.

What is an error, and why

InputWhy it is rejected
An unknown key or keyword, anywhereA typo must never weaken a schema silently.
format other than uuid, date-time, date, local-date-time, time, duration (email, uri, ...)Accepting an unknown format as a plain string now would let a later version silently change what an existing schema accepts. Remove the format (the value is a string).
formatMinimum (and the other format bounds) without a temporal format, or with text that is not of the format's typeA bound needs the type it compares in; the hint shows an example of the type's text.
